record.question:
A central employee-registry application runs in a VPC in one AWS Region. Servers in three departmental VPCs need private access to it, and the VPC CIDRs do not overlap. The security team wants source addresses for traffic rejected by security groups or network ACLs, with automated notifications in its separate security account. A short log-delivery delay is acceptable.

Which design meets these requirements with the least network-appliance administration?

options.text: Deploy and maintain VPN appliances between every departmental VPC and the central VPC. Collect REJECT VPC Flow Logs and build a central SNS notification processor.

Create VPC peering connections with appropriate routes and security rules. Send REJECT VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs, forward them through a cross-account destination to Kinesis in the security account, and process matching records to publish SNS notifications.
Create VPC peering connections and collect only ALB HTTP access logs. Notify security when an ALB log entry shows a request rejected by a security group or network ACL.
Connect the VPCs through a Transit Gateway and stream REJECT VPC Flow Logs to a central Kinesis stream. Rely on the log subscription itself to send notifications to the security team.

explanation.text:
<<2>> is correct. Peering provides direct private connectivity for this small set of nonoverlapping VPCs. Flow Logs capture network-interface traffic metadata, including recorded source addresses and REJECT actions. A supported cross-account subscription path centralizes those records, and an explicit processing and SNS step generates notifications.

<<1>> can be engineered to carry traffic and alert on logs, but adds VPN appliances, patching, and tunnel administration that peering avoids.

<<3>> relies on application-layer logs for packets rejected before reaching the ALB application path. Those logs cannot replace VPC Flow Logs for the stated network-control denials.

<<4>> supplies connectivity and transport of log records but omits the notification mechanism. A subscription delivers data to its destination, not automatically to a human recipient.

Configure return routes and security rules as well as the peering links. Flow Logs are aggregated, best-effort telemetry rather than packet capture or a guaranteed immediate alert, and REJECT is not an HTTP authorization status.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [VPC peering](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/what-is-vpc-peering.html); [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs.html); [VPC flow record fields](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-log-records.html); [Cross-account log subscriptions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CrossAccountSubscriptions.html).

diagram_alt: Peering provides private connectivity while a separate log-processing chain produces the security notification.

sources.supports: Peering provides private addressing between VPCs with traffic remaining on the AWS backbone rather than the public internet.
Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata from VPC network interfaces and can deliver it to CloudWatch Logs.
Flow records include source-address and action information, and REJECT can represent security-group or network-ACL rejection.
Cross-account log destinations can deliver records to Kinesis or Firehose for central processing and analysis.

editorial_notes: Preserved answer 2. Defined denials at the network layer, specified a concrete supported cross-account log destination, and added the required processing-to-notification step.
